y: From Proto-West Germanic *-fōtī, from Proto-Germanic *-fōtijaz. Cognate with Old High German -fuozi. Equivalent to fōt + -e.

s: having a certain number of floors: -story, -stories
y: Possibly goes back to a Proto-Germanic *flōrijaz. Equivalent to flōr + -e.
Equivalent to fōt (“foot”) + -e (adjectival suffix), but without i-mutation.
From Proto-Germanic *-fullaz (“-ful”), from Proto-Germanic *fullaz (“full”).
From Old English fæst (“secure, firm”).

s: Diminutive suffix, used especially in familiar names for pets.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-gō, from Proto-Germanic *-gjô, *-gô (suffix).

s: suffix used to denote a region or territory
suffix used in placenames meaning region of, or district of
y: From Proto-West Germanic *gawi, from Proto-Germanic *gawją, *gawjō, *gawô (“country, region, environment”).

s: Used to form verbs from nouns and adjectives, often with an intensive effect
y: From the fusion of Proto-West Germanic *-igōn, *-īgōn, *-agōn, *-ugōn, from Proto-Germanic *-gōną, equivalent to -iġ + -ian. Cognate with Old High German -igōn, -agōn, Old Norse -ga.

s: forming nouns of condition or quality, from nouns or adjectives
y: From Proto-West Germanic *haidu, from Proto-Germanic *haiduz (“state, condition”) (originally a noun, represented by Old English hād). Cognate with Old Saxon -hēd, Dutch -heid, Old High German -heit (German -heit).

s: bent; inclined toward, tending toward; sloping toward
bent to shoot downwards, precipitous, oblique, steep
y: From Proto-Germanic *halþaz (“inclined”). Akin to Old Frisian -hald, Old High German -hald, Old Norse -hallr, Old English heald (“bent, inclined toward”), Old English hielde (“slope”).
From Proto-West Germanic *-handī, from Proto-Germanic *-handijaz. Equivalent to hand + -e.
From Proto-West Germanic *-hert(ī), from Proto-Germanic *-hertaz, derived from *hertô (“heart”) (Old English heorte). Cognate with Old Saxon -hert, Old High German -herz, Gothic -𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍄𐍃 (-hairts).
From hīewian (“to form, shape”)

s: Forms adjectives from certain nouns. Often drops the initial h-, taking the form -līepe.
y: From Proto-Germanic *-hlaupijaz (“running”), used to form adjectives, derived from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną from Proto-Indo-European *klewb- (“to spring, stumble”). Cognate with Old Saxon -lōpi and Old Norse -hleypr. More at hlēapan.

s: some- (forms indefinite pronouns and adverbs from interrogatives)
y: Unknown. There are no known cognates.

s: Forms adjectives from numerals denoting the amount (in hundreds of shillings) of wergeld a person is worth.
y: From hund (“hundred”) + -e (adjectival suffix).

s: Forms demonyms from toponyms ending in -hām
Forms verbs from nouns and adjectives.
y: By syncope from earlier *-ōjan, a northern Ingvaeonic innovated form of Proto-West Germanic *-ōn, from Proto-Germanic *-ōną.

s: noun suffix denoting a female agent
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ggjā, from Proto-Germanic *-gjǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *-ikyeh₂. Cognate with Middle Low German -igge, -ige, -ege, Middle Dutch -igge, -egge (modern Dutch -egge), Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa).
From Proto-West Germanic compounds ending in *-augī (i.e. *augā (“eye”) with the adjective-forming suffix *-ī). By surface analysis, ēage + -e. Cognate with Proto-Norse ᚨᚢᚷᛁᛉ (augiʀ), Old Norse eygr.

s: Used to form the present participle of class II weak verbs
Used to form the inflected infinitive of class II weak verbs

y:

s: Used to form the first person singular present indicative of class II weak verbs

y: From Proto-West Germanic *-aht. Akin to Old Saxon -aht, Old High German -aht (German -icht), Icelandic -óttr, Old English -iġ.

A metathetic alteration of Proto-Germanic *-ikīna (diminutive suffix) + *-il- (diminutive suffix).
Alternately, from Proto-Germanic *-ingilą, *-ingilaz.

s: Forming nouns from verbs, indicating action, process or material.
y: Variant of -ung.

s: Forming derivatives of nouns with sense of ‘belonging to, son of’.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ing, from Proto-Germanic *-ingaz.
From Proto-West Germanic *-isk.

s: suffix forming nouns with a collective or group force
y: From Proto-Germanic *-iską, *-iskiją.

s: Forms nouns referring to female people. Attested only in the noun abbadisse.
y: From Late Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ῐσσᾰ (-ĭssă)

s: noun suffix denoting activity (compare Modern English -ation)
y:
From Proto-West Germanic *-laik, from Proto-Germanic *-laiką (“jump, spring, sport”) (alternative form of *-laikaz), from *laiką (“play, sport, fight, activity”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“to bounce, shake, tremble”). Related to Proto-Germanic *laikaz (“game, dance, hymn, sport”).
Akin to Old English lāc (“sport, play”). More at English lake (Etymology 2).
Also borrowed from Old Norse as Middle English -laik, -leȝȝe.
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laibō. More at Proto-Germanic *Anulaibaz.
Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-laus. Synchronically, from lēas (“false, devoid of, free from, without”).
From Proto-West Germanic *-lōn, from Proto-Germanic *-lōną, perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *-ulaz.

From Proto-West Germanic *-līk, from Proto-Germanic *-līkaz (adjectival suffix, originally meaning “having form of”), derived from *līką (“body,” earlier “form”), whence Old English līċ. Cognate with Old Frisian -lik, Old Saxon -līk, Old High German -līh, Old Norse -ligr, and Gothic -𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (-leiks).

From Proto-Germanic *-līkê, equivalent to -līċ (adjectival suffix) + -e (adverbial suffix). Compare Old Norse -liga.

s: suffix denoting lack, want or absence of: -lessness
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-lausiþu; By surface analysis, -lēas (“-less”) + -t (“-th; -ness”).
From Proto-Germanic *-lībijaz, equivalent to līf + -e.

s: adverbial suffix denoting direction, state or position
y: From alteration of suffixal use of Old English lang (“long”).

s: suffix used in forming personal nouns
Icling ("dynasty of Icel" or "House of Icel"); Ætheling (House of Ethel)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ling, from Proto-Germanic *-ilingaz.

s: by hand, hand to hand, at close range, near

y: Perhaps dates back to a Proto-Germanic *-mannijaz. Equivalent to mann + -e.

s: -most; used to form the superlative of certain words, such as cardinal directions
y: From Proto-Germanic *-umistaz, from the comparative suffix *-umô + the regular superlative suffix *-istaz
From Proto-Germanic *-mōdaz, derived from *mōdaz (“mind”) (Old English mōd). Cognate with Old Saxon -mōd, Old High German -muot.

s: used to denote a fixed amount of something at a time
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-mālum. Identical to the dative/instrumental plural of mǣl (“time, occasion”).
